reason: "Identify each of the following plants. A B C" — three photographs of weeds. The scheme answers are A = Buttercup, B = Thistle, C = Dock (leaf), 3 x 2 marks; without the images the card is a dangling reference.
"State the meaning of symbols A and B on the sign" — the two pictograms on a reproduced farm safety notice. Nothing in the text says what A and B depict.
"State the function of C and D" — two photographs of farm equipment printed on the safety notice page. Unanswerable without the images.
"In relation to picture C at part (ii) above, state one advantage of using this piece of equipment to enhance sustainability of the farm." Depends entirely on identifying the equipment in picture C.
"Identify the farm machines, labelled A and B, which are attached to each tractor" — two photographs. Scheme: A = seed drill / combine drill / one pass system, B = zero grazer.
"State one way machine A can enhance environmental sustainability." Machine A is only identifiable from the photograph in part (b)(i), so the card would ask about an unnamed machine.
"Outline one disadvantage of using machine (method) B when feeding high producing animals." Machine B is only identifiable from the photograph in part (b)(i).
"Identify one way in which the farm in the photograph could become more energy efficient." The whole question is anchored to an aerial photograph of a farm layout that has not been extracted.

"State two ways in which the farmyard is suited to economy of labour." Every scheme answer reads off the photograph (sheds situated close together, silage bales and pit close to the sheds, cow housing close to parlour).

"Suggest two ways in which the farmer could make the farmyard more environmentally sustainable." Scheme answers name features of the photograph (the bank beside the shed, the collecting yard, the open lagoon).
Tick-box identification of a plant shown only as a photograph (scheme: 'Oilseed rape*'). Nothing in the text identifies it.
Tick-box identification of a plant shown only as a photograph (scheme: 'Barley*').
Tick-box identification of a plant shown only as a photograph (scheme: 'Clover*').
'Identify each of the following plants commonly found in grassland' — four photographs labelled A–D (daisy, dock leaf, buttercup, thistle). Pure image identification.
'Describe one method used to kill plant B.' Plant B is identifiable only from the photograph in (b)(i), so the card would carry a dangling reference. Should be authored in the same wave as (b)(i).
'Identify the labelled parts A, B, C on the diagram using the correct word from the list' — labels on a diagram of the sheep digestive system (rumen, abomasum, omasum).
'Identify the two types of soils shown in profile diagrams A and B' — brown earth and podzol, distinguishable only from the two profile drawings.
'Outline one use for soil A.' Which profile is soil A comes only from the diagram, so a text-only card cannot say what soil is being asked about.
'Describe two disadvantages associated with the use of soil B.' The scheme's answers are podzol-specific (iron pan, leaching); the student can only know B is a podzol from the profile diagram.
'What is meant by this farm safety sign?' — the sign is an image (overhead power lines / electric shock risk).
'Explain this farm safety sign.' — the sign is an image (moving farm machinery).
'Where would you rank the greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture in 2018?' — answered by reading agriculture's 34% slice on the EPA pie chart printed on the paper.
'Name the part labelled A on the diagram' — label on the cow reproductive-tract diagram (scheme: 'Ovary*').
'Outline the function of the part labelled A.' Which structure A is comes only from the diagram.
'Indicate by placing an X on the diagram exactly where the top of the insemination gun needs to be positioned' — the answer is a mark made on the diagram, not a phrase.
'Identify the structure located at B' on the 3D farmyard plan (scheme: silage pit).
'Describe one environmental hazard and one potential safety hazard of structure B.' Structure B is identified only from the 3D plan.
'Outline one way in which the farmyard layout is economically sustainable.' The scheme credits observations read off the layout (buildings close together, good access roads).
'Explain how one named piece of new technology could enhance economy of labour on this farm.' 'This farm' is defined only by the 3D plan, so the part travels with (a)(i)–(iii).
'Place an X on the plan view above to show one place where you would advise Claire and John to install slatted tanks. Give a reason for your answer.' The 2-mark placement is a mark on the plan.
'Identify each breed using the list of names' — four photographs of cattle and sheep breeds (Charolais, Limousin, Jacob, Border Leicester).

'Identify any four of the following breeds of animals' with six photographs labelled A–F (scheme: A = Landrace, B = Blue Leicester, C = Connemara (pony), D = Rhode Island red, E = Limousine, F = (Holstein) Friesian — 4(1), 4 marks). Unanswerable without the images, and no figures have been extracted for agricultural science yet, so a text-only card would be a dangling reference. Pick up in a figure wave: the crop needed is page 5 of the 2022 HL paper, the six-photo breed grid.

'Draw a labelled diagram of a calf's stomach in its first week of life' (6 marks: D = 3, 2, 0 for the drawing plus L = 3(1) for any three labels). The scheme band-marks the drawing and never names the labels, so there are no discrete text marking points to tick — transcribing 'Candidates diagram must clearly show all four chambers...' would be a criterion, not an answer. The MarkBank row model deliberately excludes band rubrics until a renderer exists. Would need a reference diagram of the four-chambered calf stomach plus a named label key before it can be carded.

'Identify and state the function of machine A and B' — both machines are only identifiable from the two photographs. No figures extracted for this subject yet, so a text-only card would be a dangling reference. Scheme rows on disk: A = (fertiliser) spreader / Function = spread (shake or broadcast) fertiliser / spreading grass seed / B = Slurry spreader or slurry tanker or trailing shoe or injector / Function = spreading slurry or effluent, 2+2+2+2 = 8 marks.

'Identify any three of the following breeds' — A, B, C and D are four photographs of cattle, pigs and sheep. Pure photo identification. Scheme: A = Simmental / B = Landrace / C = Blackface mountain or Swaledale / D = Jersey, tariff 3(2) = 6 marks.
'Identify breed E and F' — two ram photographs. Pure photo identification. Scheme: E = Border Leister / F = Texel or Beltex, tariff 3+1 = 4 marks.

'Advise Jessica with reasons which breed to choose' — depends on identifying breeds E and F from the photographs, and the scheme prints two separate answer pools (one for E, one for F) at 3+1 = 4 marks total, so a single card cannot carry both routes without inflating the tariff. Needs the figure plus a route-aware card model.

'Identify the safety symbols labelled A and B above' — the two GHS pictograms are images on the paper. Scheme: A = Health hazard / carcinogenic (2), B = Harmful / caution / danger / warning / irritant (2) = 4 marks.

'Identify what A, B and C are representing in the picture illustrating photosynthesis' — A, B and C are arrows on a labelled plant diagram. Scheme: A = Carbon dioxide (CO2) / B = Oxygen (O2) or water vapour / C = Glucose (C6H12O6) or oxygen or water vapour, tariff 4+1+1 = 6 marks.
'Identify each piece of equipment A and B above' — two laboratory-equipment photographs. Scheme: A = Inoculating loop (2), B = Petri dish or agar plate (2) = 4 marks.

'Identify each of the following breeds of animals' — A, B and C are photographs of cattle printed on page 3 of the paper (the scheme gives A – Short horn, B – Belgian Blue, C – Simmental, 3(2) = 6 marks). Unanswerable without the images, so a text-only card would be a dangling reference.
'Identify each of the following breeds of animals' — D, E and F are photographs on page 4 (scheme: D – Jersey, E – Suffolk, F – Texel, 3(2) = 6 marks). Same figure dependency as (a)(i).

'Identify any two of the weeds that can be found in Irish fields using the list below' — page 5 of the paper carries three ~473x350 photographs of weeds to be matched against the printed name list (Chickweed, Charlock, Shepard's Purse). The scheme answer is 'Shepherd's purse Chickweed Charlock 2(2)', which is meaningless without seeing which photograph is which.

'Analyse the graph and briefly describe the conclusion the student made from his investigation.' The scheme's answer quotes values read off the printed bar chart (250mg/l unprotected urea vs 50mg/l protected urea) which are not in the paper's text. Needs the graph crop.

'Label the diagram below of the monogastric digestive system' — A, B and C on a 1350x946 diagram on page 14 (scheme: A: Liver, B: Stomach, C: Small intestine, 3(2) = 6 marks). A labelling question with no diagram is exactly the failure this tool exists to prevent.

"Identify any two pieces of equipment labelled A, B or C required for this investigation." The candidate names equipment shown in the paper's photograph (scheme: A = pH paper or (universal) indicator paper, B = graduated cylinder, C = electronic or mass balance, 2(3) = 6 marks). A text-only card would be a dangling reference to a picture that has not been extracted for this subject.

"State the pH of the soil filtrate." The answer (6.5*, 3 marks, asterisked so only the exact value scores) is read off the pH probe / universal indicator shown in the paper's photograph. Not answerable from text alone.

"Identify the best quality silage and state for which animals this silage is suitable." The answer ("Best quality silage = 76%+ DMD or A", 2 marks; "Suitable animals = freshly calved dairy cows in winter milk", 1 mark) is read off the paper's grass-growth-cycle diagram, whose DMD bands are lettered A-D. The lettered band cannot be resolved without the figure.
"State which silage DMD % is suitable for dry suckler cows that have a good BCS." Answer "<67(%) or D", 1 mark — a specific band read off the same lettered DMD table in the paper's diagram.
"Identify the stomach chamber A." Answer "Abomasum*", 3 marks, asterisked. The letter A is on the paper's ruminant-stomach diagrams; without the figure the question has no referent.

"Identify the items of farm machinery or equipment shown in A, B and C" — the three items (bale wrapper, stomach tube, head gate / fostering crate) exist only as photographs on the paper. No figures have been extracted for Agricultural Science yet, so a text-only card would be a dangling reference. Tariff 3(2) = 6 marks; part (b) of the same question IS carded.

"Identify any two of the following breeds" — A Landrace, B Blue Leicester, C Simmental are shown only as breed photographs. Tariff 2(2) = 4 marks. Parts (a)(ii) and (a)(iii) are carded, with the breed identities supplied as editor context.

"Based on your knowledge of soil structure, identify the soil quality of each of the different soils in A, B and C" — the three soils are photographs of soil structure, and the judgement is entirely visual. Tariff 3(2) = 6 marks. Part (b)(ii) is carded.
"Identify which picture A or B is more likely to be a multi-species (polyculture) sward" — answer is "B", readable only from the two sward photographs. Tariff 4 marks. Parts (b) and (c) are carded.

The answer is a tick showing which way the grazing arrow points in the strip-grazing diagram. Nothing is answerable without the diagram, and the scheme prints no answer text — only the tick in the correct box.
"Label A in the diagram." The answer '(Moveable)(Electric) Fence' is a label on a specific part of the strip-grazing diagram, which has not been extracted.
"Identify the type of grazing system shown in the diagram." Answer 'Strip grazing' is read directly off the diagram; a text-only card would give the answer away or be unanswerable.

"Briefly explain one reason why handling facility B is better for animal movement." The scheme's answer turns on the curved race in picture B versus the straight 'wrong way' race in picture A; without the two photographs the comparison has no referent.
"Label any three parts of the diagram" (A–D on the calf's ruminant digestive system: Omasum, Rumen, Abomasum, Reticulum). Pure figure-labelling — 3(2) = 6 marks awaiting the diagram.
"Identify any three of the following breeds" from photographs A–D (Charolais, Border Leicester, Texel, Suffolk). Pure photo identification — 3(2) = 6 marks awaiting the images.
"In step 2, state which hen A, B or C is the best offspring to breed future generations." The answer 'A' can only be reached by reading the egg numbers on each hen in the selective-breeding diagram.

"State with reason which cow A or B a farmer would choose to cross with the Belgian Blue bull." The scheme's answer 'Cow: B or Charolais / Reason: Big frame / continental breed / wide pelvis' depends on seeing the two cow photographs.
'Identify both cattle breeds in A and B.' The two breeds are only shown as photographs (scheme: A: Aberdeen Angus, B: Hereford, 5+1). Unanswerable as text; needs the paper's two breed images.

'State which breed A or B has a dominant polled trait as a characteristic of the breed' (2 marks, answer 'A or Aberdeen Angus'). The student cannot know which photograph is A without seeing them, so the question dangles without the figure. The 2-mark part (c) that follows was carded because it only explains the term 'polled'.

'Identify the three pieces of equipment needed for lambing from the six images below' (3x1 names + 3x1 identified = 6 marks). Answers are letter-keyed to six photographs (A: Stomach tube / C: heat lamp / D: ropes). Needs the six-image plate. Part (b) was carded separately since it carries its own 4-mark tariff and is answerable in words.

Photo-identification: 'Identify any three breeds A, B, C or D using the list below' over four cattle photographs. Answer key is A: Charolais / B: Jersey / C: Limousin / D: Holstein Friesian, tariff 3x2 = 6 (any three of the four at 2 each — a bestNofParts card, not a fixed one). Unanswerable and unmarkable without the four crops.

'Suggest two ways in which this farm allows for efficient labour' is read off an aerial photograph of a dairy farm layout; every scheme answer (paddocks near yard, roadways for access, sheds near farmhouse, silage storage near sheds) is an observation about that specific photograph. Tariff 3+2 = 5. Scheme pool ends 'any two valid examples', so the future card needs openList.
'Identify which structure A, B or C is most suitable for slurry storage' — answer 'A', 3 marks — requires the labelled photograph, and the paper's response mode is marking an X on the image itself.

'Suggest why this farm may be suited to either method of grazing' (2 marks); the scheme's answers (paddocks adjacent for rotational grazing, roadways for access, little or no hedgerows, farmyard central to the fields) all describe features of the photograph.

'Identify with reason which picture A, B, or C has the ideal soil composition' over three pie-style soil composition diagrams. Tariff 3+2 = 5 (Picture 3, Reason 2). The reason ('seedling is largest in picture B', '25% air or 25% water') is a direct reading of the figure.

'Outline one reason why soil C has a high percentage of mineral and organic matter' (2 marks) names a lettered element of the same soil-composition diagram; carding it text-only would leave 'soil C' dangling.

Photo-identification: 'Identify any three plants shown in the table' over four plant photographs. Answer key A: (Perennial) ryegrass / B: (White) clover / C: Nettle / D: Chicory, tariff 3x2 = 6 (any three of four at 2 each — bestNofParts).

'Choose the two warning signs by placing a tick in the correct boxes to identify these signs' — answer 'Symbols 2 and 3', tariff 3+2 = 5. The hazard pictograms exist only as images; there is no text form of the options.

'Identify with reason which picture A or B is the correct position for a calf at birth' over two calf-presentation drawings. Tariff 3+2 = 5 (Picture 3, Reason 2); the reason ('Fore or front legs first with head lying flat on top of legs') describes what is drawn.
'Identify the sex cell labelled A' on the sex-sorting diagram — answer 'Sperm or male', 3 marks. A labelling question with no diagram is exactly the failure the deck guard blocks.
'Identify the main cause of lamb mortality' — answer 'Abortion and stillbirth', 3 marks — is read off the bar chart of causes; the bar heights are not present as text.

'Complete the graph above to show that 20% of lambs die due to disease' — the scheme's answer is 'Bar inserted in graph to height of 20', 2 marks. Needs the chart, and also needs a drawing-response renderer that Mark Bank's tick model does not yet have.
'Identify which lamb (single or twin) had a higher growth rate over the 25 weeks' — answer 'Single', 3 marks — is read off the lamb growth-rate line graph.
'Predict which lamb will have a higher weight at slaughter' — answer 'Single', 3 marks — extrapolates the same growth-rate graph; without the plotted lines there is nothing to predict from.

'Identify each of the following cattle and sheep breeds' over four photographs labelled A, B, C, D (scheme: A = Suffolk, B = Shorthorn, C = Belgian blue, D = Texel, 4(1)). The answers are meaningless without the images, and the build additionally drops any card whose questionText names lettered parts and carries no labelled figure. No agricultural-science figures have been extracted yet.

'Identify which treatment is the most beneficial organic fertiliser for a steady supply of herbage over the five month period' is answered by reading the printed line graph of total available kg DM/ha for five treatments across November to March. The scheme's answer ('FYM ‐ High', 3 marks) cannot be reasoned to from text alone, and unlike the Q14(c) report the graph is not a data table that can be reproduced faithfully in a stem.

A calculation read straight off the same graph (3+2 marks), comparing the increase in kg DM/ha for the chosen treatment against the control. The scheme gives two accepted solutions using values lifted from the graph (3700 - 1400, 3400 - 1000 etc.); without the graph the student cannot check where those numbers come from.

'Using evidence from the data, outline the advice you would give him in relation to the source and application rates of organic fertiliser' (4 marks). The scheme's answer is anchored to a graph reading — 'The highest Kg DM per ha availability in Feb for early turnout in spring was in the FYM High (25 ton / ha) treatment as there was 3200 kg DM per ha available for grazing' — so a text-only card would be a dangling reference to the figure.

Three specific recommendations, 3(2) = 6 marks, where the scheme states outright 'All statements above must be backed up by relevant evidence from graph'. Every marking point is a comparison between plotted treatment lines (FYM v slurry, high v low rates, March availability), so the part is unanswerable and unmarkable without the graph.

Calculate which farmer (Dan or Joe) earns a higher price for their milk. The whole task is arithmetic on the paper's printed payment table (supply in litres and kg, protein and fat percentages and kilograms for each farmer, the €5.48/kg protein and €3.35/kg fat prices, the €0.04/litre processing deduction, and Joe's already-computed €9,316 and €6,830 lines). The scheme's answer is the worked calculation itself (1803 x 5.48 = 9880.44 ... Total = 15,558.64 against Joe's 14,146), which is meaningless without the table it operates on. Worth 6 marks (4 for correct totals, 2 for naming Dan) — bind the table crop and this becomes a strong card.

Determine the P and K soil indexes for field 2. This is table-reading twice over: the candidate must take field 2's P result (6.42 mg/l) and K result (157 mg/l) off one printed table and look each up against the printed Reference Soil Index table (P index 3 = 5.1-8.0 mg/l, K index 4 = 151 mg/l and above) to reach the scheme's 'P = 3 / K = 4 (both answers must be correct for 3 marks)'. Without both tables on screen there is nothing to determine. 3 marks.

Reads 'Which county has the highest % fluke damage?' against a printed county map of liver fluke damage to beef cattle livers (Q3 2020 Beef HealthCheck data). The scheme's answer is 'Louth* (at 17%)' — unreachable without reading the map, so a text-only card would be a dangling reference. 4 marks.

'Complete the graph below by plotting the percentage germination of the grass seeds at 20°C as calculated at part (a) and at 30°C.' The answer is a plotting act on the printed bar chart ('Correct bar drawn at 20oC up to 60', 'Correct bar drawn at 30oC up to 65'), which cannot be ticked off a text-only card. Worth 3+3 = 6 marks.

'The following are pictures of two beef cattle breeds... State one physical trait, in either of the animals above, and give one reason why this trait is an advantage to beef farmers.' The trait is to be read off the two breed photographs, so a text-only card leaves a dangling reference. Worth 2+2 = 4 marks. (Scheme answers exist and are transcribable — 'polled (no horns)' / 'less dangerous' — so this becomes cardable the moment the figure is extracted.)

'Using the graph, determine the minimum number of weeks for the lambs to reach this liveweight.' The question instructs the candidate to read the printed liveweight graph, and the scheme's answer is '14 ( can be indicated on the graph)'. Worth 4 marks.

'Identify which treatment group had the greatest effect on plant growth.' The answer ('All nutrients (NPK)') is read off the printed bar chart of mean shoot length by treatment group; the chart's series-to-value mapping could not be reconstructed from the extracted text with certainty, so it is not inlined. Worth 2 marks.

Pure photograph identification — 'Identify any two of the following plants A, B or C from the sward', where A, B and C are three photographs printed on page 20 of the paper. The scheme's answers (A = Italian ryegrass, B = Chicory, C = Cocksfoot) are meaningless without the images. 2 marks (2(1)).

'Identify the growth cycle stage of the plants in part (iii) and describe briefly what happens at this stage.' Both halves dangle on the same three photographs: the stage ('Reproductive stage') can only be read off the pictured seed heads, and the description row credits 'wind pollination occurs in A or insect pollination occurs in B', which names the lettered photographs directly. Naming A/B/C in a stem would not fix it, because the plant names alone do not tell a student what growth stage the plants were photographed at. 6 marks (3 + 3).

'Analyse the picture of calf housing below … Identify three aspects of the shed which make it a suitable environment for calves and provide a reason for each aspect identified.' The scheme's answers name features of the pictured shed specifically (space sheeting or high roof, board or concrete walls, clean roof lights, large lying area, clean bedding, long feed barrier), so the whole part hangs on the photograph on page 25 of the paper. 9 marks (3(3)).

'Complete the diagram using arrows to show the natural airflow he should expect through the shed.' The student annotates a printed cross-section of the shed, and the scheme's answer ('Correct indication of arrows coming in at side / going out through roof') is a judgement about marks drawn on that diagram. 5 marks (4 + 1).

'Using the Integrated Management System for controlling weeds (outlined on previous page), provide advice to them on the future of weed control on their farms', 3(4) = 12 marks. The question sends the candidate to the Teagasc IMS diagram printed on the previous page, which has not been extracted for this subject. Separately, the scheme's answer is a two-column table (IMS component -> advice) whose left column — Integrated Management, Use of herbicides, Increased seed rates, Cover crops, Competitive crops, Rogueing, Crop rotation, Whole cropping, Crop destruction, On-farm hygiene, Machinery hygiene — is interleaved into the middle of the right-hand advice text by the PDF extractor, so not one marking point can be transcribed with its component name intact. Both reasons independently rule the card out.

"Sketch onto the photograph of field A below, the pattern the farmer would use when taking a number of soil samples." The whole answer ("W shape on photograph", 4 marks) is a mark made on the photograph printed in the paper, and no figures have been extracted for Agricultural Science, so a text-only card would be a dangling reference to an image the student cannot see.

Requires the printed grass-growth curve AND is a drawing task on it: 'Shade onto the graph above the portion which represents the excess grass in summer months.' The scheme answer ('Shaded area between continous blue line and orange dash line') is meaningless without the two plotted lines. No figure extracted for this subject yet.
'Identify each of the plants A and B' — the plants exist only as photographs on page 31. The scheme answers (Ragwort; Plantain or Ribwort) cannot be reached from text.
'State one impact plant A has on farming or the environment.' Plant A is identifiable only from the photograph, so the card would be answerless without it, even though the scheme's answers are text.
'Identify each of the following plants commonly found on Irish farms' — plants C and D are photographs only (scheme: Thistle; Oats (wild)).
'State one use for plant D.' Plant D (wild oats) is identifiable only from the photograph.

'Calculate the total bovine nitrogen (figure A) for John's 1-2 year-old cattle' — the multipliers (40 livestock, 57 kg N) come only from the printed bovine-nitrogen data table, and the answer cell is the lettered item A. Note for a later pass: this table is plain text/numbers, not an image, so if the deck ever supports an inlined data table in the stem, Q17(b)(i)-(iii) become 20 further marks of good cards.

'Calculate the total bovine nitrogen (figure B) for all animals on John's farm' — the five addends (2990, 1056, 2280, 57, 65) come from the printed data table and the answer cell is the lettered item B.
'State if John achieved his target of 5% bovine nitrogen reduction.' The comparison depends on figure B, which is only obtainable from the printed data table in (b)(ii).

'Identify which variety of perennial ryegrass produces the highest yield.' The scheme answer (Moyola, 105 t DM/ha) is read straight off the printed DAFM variety table; without it the card has no data to analyse.
'Identify which variety would produce more grass in autumn.' Same printed DAFM variety table (scheme: Moyola, 107); unanswerable as text.

Asks the candidate to identify the soil water content level for each of three soil-sample diagrams labelled A, B and C printed in the paper (brown = soil particles, blue = water, white = air spaces). The scheme's answer is positional (A: Saturation / B: Permanent wilting point / C: Field capacity), so without the figure the card would be an unanswerable dangling reference. Worth 3(3) = 9 marks; card it once the figure is extracted.

Requires reading the bar chart 'Effect of soil pH on nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions' printed in the paper to pick the pH with the lowest cumulative emissions. The scheme answer is the starred value '*6.9', which cannot be derived from text alone. Worth 6 marks; card it once the graph is extracted.

Asks the candidate to discuss the relationship between pH and N2O emissions 'on the graph' and its implications for farming practice, so it depends on the same bar chart as (c)(i). Worth 5 + 3 = 8 marks; card it once the graph is extracted.

'Identify the main source of carbon emissions on the farm.' The answer (*Animal digestion) is read straight off the Bord Bia bar chart of percentage share by source. The bar values are not extractable text and no figure has been bound for this subject, so a text-only card would be unanswerable.

'State with reason if the main source of emissions is above or below the national average for the enterprise.' The scheme's answer ('Below' / 'As the average for the enterprise is over 40% / is less for the current and previous assessments') is a direct read of the graph's national-average series against the farm's bars.

'Comment on the overall carbon emissions on the farm since Anna and Lucy joined the scheme and justify your answer.' Requires comparing the 2021 and 2019 assessment series bar by bar against the national average, including 'correct use of percentages from graph'.

'Identify any two of the plant species commonly found in Irish multi species seed mixtures.' The paper prints three photographs labelled A, B and C and the scheme answers them as A = Perennial ryegrass or PRG, B = (Ribwort) plantain, C = Chicory. Pure photo identification.

'Label any three parts of the structure of the udder.' The paper prints an udder diagram with leader lines A, B, C and D; the scheme is a label key (A Teat, B Median suspensory ligament, C Connective tissue / fine membrane, D Epidermis / hind quarter / outer wall). Unanswerable without the labelled diagram, and the build gate also refuses a lettered-parts question that carries no bound figure.

'Assist Jenny in placing each step in the correct order by matching the correct letter to the number in the box.' The four California Mastitis Test steps are printed as a lettered picture-and-caption grid (A-D) and the scheme answer is the ordering '1 A 2 D 3 B 4 C'. The letters must be decoded from the paper's figure.

Pure identification from the paper's three plant photographs — the scheme's answers are 'A: Red clover / B: Perennial ryegrass / C: White clover' (6+3+3 = 12 marks), which cannot be asked without the pictures. No figures have been extracted for Agricultural Science yet. The three identities are carried in the stem of the Q13(a)(iii) card so that part's reference to 'plants A and C' is not dangling.
Answer is 'Disc' (6 marks), read straight off the paper's bar chart comparing plough, disc, one pass and direct drill. Unanswerable without the graph.

Asks for the conclusion the researchers can draw, and the scheme's answer explicitly references the data ('correct ranking in relation to sustainability (using data from graph)', 2 marks). Unanswerable without the graph.

'State which diagram A, B or C has a higher biodiversity level and give a reason' — the scheme answers 'Diagram: C' plus reasons drawn from what is drawn in that diagram (4 + 4 marks). Unanswerable without the three farm diagrams.
Asks about 'the crop X being sown between the cows and the river in diagram A' — the lettered crop and its position exist only in the diagram (4 marks).

'State which diagram represents farming in the least environmentally friendly way and give two reasons' — the scheme answers 'Diagram: B' plus two reasons about what is drawn there (4 + 2(4) = 12 marks). Unanswerable without the diagrams.

'Identify which soil is compacted and give a reason' — the scheme answers 'Soil sample – B' with the reason 'less (air) spaces or soil particles closer together' (5 + 5 marks), both read off the two soil-particle diagrams. Unanswerable without them.

'Assist Brian in labelling the diagram' of a brown earth profile — the scheme answers 'A: Top Soil / B: Sub soil' (6+4 = 10 marks) against letters printed on the paper's soil-profile drawing. Unanswerable without it. Its alternative, part (c), is carded instead.

'Identify the plants A, B, C and D using the list below.' The paper prints four photographs labelled A–D and the scheme answer is simply the mapping A=Primrose, B=Nettle, C=Ragwort, D=Meadow Thistle. Without the four images the card is a dangling reference — nothing on it tells the student which plant is which. Worth 4(2) = 8 marks, so this is the single largest gap in the Q13 coverage and should be re-carded once agricultural-science figures are extracted and inspected.

'Calculate the average (mean) daily liveweight gain of the calves from birth to 15 weeks.' The two numbers the calculation starts from (125 kg at 15 weeks, 40 kg at birth) are only readable off the printed bar chart 'Average Liveweight Gain of Dairy Beef Calves', which the question explicitly points at ('shown in the graph below', 'Analyse the graph'). Worth 6 marks. Re-card once the graph is extracted and inspected.

"Based on the results shown, state if there is any difference in colostrum quality when pooled." The answer ("Pooled colostrum is best or valid comparison with Sample 2 or Sample 3") requires reading the IgG / birthweight / weaning-weight results table printed in the paper. No figure has been extracted for this subject, so a text-only card would be a dangling reference.

"Outline advice Ella and Sadie would give to farmers based on the results of their investigation." The 4-mark answer compares the three treatment groups' weaning weights, which only exist in the results table printed in the paper.
"Calculate A the % soil organic matter in the peat sample." The scheme's working is 55.2/90 X 100 = 61.3(%); the 55.2 g loss in mass is only given in the results table printed in the paper.
"Calculate B the % soil organic carbon in the peat sample." Depends on value A from the same results table (61.3 x 0.58 = 35.55 or 36%), which is not available without the table.
"Identify the breeds shown in A and B." A and B are photographs of cattle printed in the paper; the answers (Hereford, Holstein Friesian) cannot be reached without seeing them.
"List two dominant features from parents in A and B in part (ii) above that are passed to the offspring C." Depends on three photographs (parents A and B, offspring C) printed in the paper.

"Using the information shown in the diagram on IPM, advise farmers on ways they can reduce chemical inputs on their farm." The 16-mark answer is structured around the IPM pyramid diagram printed in the paper (Chemical / Biological / Physical-Mechanical / Cultural-Sanitation / Prevention). Worth re-carding as a diagram card once that figure is extracted — it is the single largest part in these three questions.

Asks 'Identify any three of the plants' from four photographs labelled A-D printed in the paper; the scheme answers A: Nettle / B: Dock leaf / C: Clover / D: Perennial Ryegrass. Without the images the letters are dangling references. 12 marks (3(4)).

'Calculate the average % frequency A for the dock leaf' — the 4-of-10 quadrat count can only be read off the results table printed in the paper, and the scheme's answer (4/10 x 100/1 = 40%) is meaningless without it. 6 marks.

'Identify the most suitable chart or graph ... by placing a tick in the correct box' — options A, B and C are three chart images. The scheme's entry is a tick mark on image B with no answer text at all, so it is also a tariff-only row under LAW 3. 6 marks.

'Identify the best time of the year to cut grass for silage by placing an X on the diagram' — the answer is an X on the seasonal grass-growth curve printed in the paper. The scheme's entire entry is the single character 'X', which is a tariff/placement instruction and not an answer (LAW 3). 3 marks.

'Identify the correct stage of cutting the grass for silage by placing a tick in the correct box' — A and B are two photographs of grass swards. The scheme's entry is a tick under image B with no answer text. 2 marks.

'Briefly outline one reason for your choice in part (i)' — the creditable answer depends on which photograph the candidate ticked in (b)(i) (the scheme adds 'Allow opposite points for A'), so the card cannot stand alone without both images. 2 marks.
'Identify the growth stage of plant B' — plant B is one of the two grass photographs from (b)(i). The answer (Vegetative) is text, but 'plant B' is a dangling reference without the image. 2 marks.

'Label the diagram of the ewe reproductive system' — A, B, C and D are leader lines on a diagram printed in the paper (A Uterus, B Fallopian tube, C Ovary, D Cervix). Unanswerable without the labelled figure. 12 marks (4(3)).

'Using the colours in the box below, list the colours in order of sequence used by the farmer during mating' — the box is three photographs of raddle tubs labelled A (green), B (blue), C (yellow), and the scheme answers as 'Yellow / C', 'Green / A', 'Blue / B'. The letter half of every answer is a dangling reference without the photographs. 6 marks (4 + 1 + 1).

The question is 'Identify the breed of dairy cow shown in the picture below.' and the scheme answers '(Holstein) Friesian' (6 marks). The answer can only be read off the photograph printed on the paper, and no figures have been extracted for Agricultural Science yet, so a text-only card would be a dangling reference. Card it in a later figure wave once the crop is extracted and inspected.

'Identify the hormone labelled X responsible for milk let down.' The paper prints a picture of the cow/udder with the hormone marked 'Hormone X'; the scheme answer is Oxytocin. Text-only the letter X decodes to nothing, and the build's lettered-parts guard would drop the card anyway (it names 'labelled X' with no bound figure). Worth 5 marks.

'Identify which soil A or B is most compacted and outline a reason for your answer.' A and B are the two halves of a photograph of crop growth in compacted vs uncompacted soil; the scheme answer is 'Soil: B' with the reason 'hard pan or little space for roots to grow'. Nothing in the text says which of A or B is which. Worth 10 marks (6+4).

'Calculate the % available water in a silt loam soil.' The scheme's working is '30 – 10 = 20%' — both figures are read off the paper's graph of water availability by soil type (field capacity and permanent wilting point bars for silt loam). Without the graph the numbers have no source. Worth 6 marks.

'Identify any three common plants found on Irish farms in the photographs below.' Pure photo-identification of four plants A–D (scheme key: A cleavers, B chicory, C silverweed, D oilseed rape), 3x1. Unanswerable and unmarkable without the four crops.

'Using the diagram below, outline the advice you would give them under the following headings: types of weed control; negative effects of weed control on farms; safety considerations...'. The question names the diagram explicitly and the scheme even credits 'any valid qualified description of a point from diagram'. Separately, its 4x4 tariff spreads sixteen printed marking points across three headings ('One point under each heading and the fourth point from any heading'), which cannot be represented inside the five-row cap without distorting the structure. Worth 16 marks — the single biggest part left uncarded.

Figure-dependent. The part reads "Identify which method of soil sampling A, B or C she should carry out and explain one reason why she should use this method", and the paper prints three photographs of a field overlaid with three different sampling paths (a zig-zag, scattered crosses, a W). The scheme's answer is "Method: C" plus a reason about that pattern; neither the choice nor the reason is answerable without seeing the three pictures. Worth 9 marks (5 + 4).

Figure-dependent. "The photographs below J, K and L show three common crops grown in Ireland. Identify any two of these crops" — the answer (J: Maize, K: Wheat, L: Oilseed rape) can only be reached by looking at the three photographs, which are not extracted. Worth 8 marks (4 + 4).

Figure-dependent. The paper prints a pie chart of average milk composition with two of its segments lettered A and B, and asks the candidate to identify them (scheme: A = (Butter) fat, B = Water). The segment values do appear as extracted text, but matching a value to the letter A or B depends on the chart's layout, which is an inference rather than a transcription — exactly the "items labelled A/B/C" case. Worth 6 marks (4 + 2).

Figure-dependent. "The photographs below show four stages of calf nutrition from birth to six weeks old. Place each step in the correct order" — the answer is the letter sequence D – A – B – C, which refers to four lettered photographs that are not extracted. Worth 8 marks (4x2).

"Identify three things that make the housing in the photograph suitable for beef animals" (10 marks, 4+4+2). Every scheme answer — slatted floor / rubber mats / natural lighting / straw bedding / adequate space in pens / (adequate) feeding space / good ventilation / high roof for good air circulation / headlock gates / pen gates — is read off the photograph of the beef shed on page 28. Unanswerable as a text-only card.

"The DM% of typical forage crops is shown below in the table. Identify which DM% represents Tom's silage, by placing a tick in the correct box" (6 marks, answer 25%). The forage-crop DM table is printed as an image on page 30 and did not extract as text, so the card would carry a dangling "shown below in the table" reference even though the three tick-box options (25% / 45% / 65%) are text.

"Describe how a student would show that flocculation has occurred in a soil by arranging the steps of the investigation shown below in the correct order" (16 marks, 4x4). The scheme's entire answer is the letter sequence "D - A - B - C", and the letters are bound to four photographed test-tube boxes by page layout, not by printed text. A text-only card would show a bare letter string with nothing to attach it to. (The four step captions themselves ARE text, and are reproduced in the stems of the (b)(iii) and (b)(iv) cards, which is what makes those two answerable.)

"Identify the dairy product which decreased in exports between 2015 and 2021" (6 marks, answer Infant food). Read directly off the Bord Bia bar chart of Irish dairy exports on page 36; only the axis labels and category names extracted, not the bar values.

"Using the graph, estimate the value of Irish butter exports to Ireland in 2021" (6 marks, answer 265,000 to 275,000). The answer is a reading off the same bar chart; the question names the graph explicitly and cannot be answered without it.
